arml-2003-power-01a.title: The set $\{1,2\}$
arml-2003-power-01a.body: Take $\{a,b\}=\{1,2\}$. A Fibonacci set containing $1$ must have $x_1=1$ (every later term exceeds $x_1\ge1$, so exceeds $1$). Since $x_2\ge2$ and $x_3=x_1+x_2\ge3$, the member $2$ must be $x_2$. So the set is $\{1,2,3,5,\dots\}$, the only Fibonacci set containing $\{1,2\}$. ∎

arml-2003-power-02a.title: Look at the term after 8
arml-2003-power-02a.body:
Let $x$ be the term of $F$ immediately after $8$. Then the members after $8$ are $x,\ 8+x,\ 8+2x,\ 16+3x,\ 24+5x,\ 40+8x,\ 64+13x,\dots$ and $x>8$. Since $x>8$, $64+13x>168>144$, so $144$ equals one of the first six: $x=144$, $136$, $68$, $\frac{128}3$ (not an integer), $24$, or $13$ from $144=x$, $8+x$, $8+2x$, $16+3x$, $24+5x$, $40+8x$ respectively. Hence $x\in\{144,136,68,24,13\}$.

If $x\ge24$ then the term before $8$ would be $x-8\ge16>8$, impossible; so $8$ is the first term and $F=\{8,x,\ldots\}$: $\{8,144,\ldots\}$, $\{8,136,\ldots\}$, $\{8,68,\ldots\}$, $\{8,24,\ldots\}$.

If $x=13$, going backwards from $8,13$ the previous terms are $5,3,2,1$ (each is the difference of the next two). One step further back would need a term $1$ before the $1$, giving the first two terms $1,1$, which is not allowed since $x_1<x_2$. So the set may start at $8$, $5$, $3$, $2$ or $1$: $\{8,13,\ldots\}$, $\{5,8,\ldots\}$, $\{3,5,\ldots\}$, $\{2,3,\ldots\}$, $\{1,2,\ldots\}$.

That is $4+5=9$ sets. ∎

arml-2003-power-02b.title: Two directions
arml-2003-power-02b.body:
**Lemma (no members in between).** If $x<y$ are members of a Fibonacci set $F$ and $y\le2x$, then no member of $F$ lies strictly between them (so $x,y$ are consecutive members). *Proof.* Let $x=x_i$, $y=x_l$ and suppose $x_i<x_k<x_l$ for some $k$. Then $i<k<l$, and $y=x_l\ge x_{k+1}=x_k+x_{k-1}\ge x_k+x_i>2x$, contradicting $y\le2x$.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $b\ne2a$. The set $F_1=\{a,b,\ldots\}$ contains $a,b$. If $b<2a$, then $0<b-a<a$ and $F_2=\{b-a,a,\ldots\}$ has $x_3=b$, so it also contains $\{a,b\}$ (and $F_2\ne F_1$). If $b>2a$, then $a<b-a<b$ and $F_2=\{a,b-a,\ldots\}$ has $x_3=b$ (and $F_2\ne F_1$ since $x_2$ differs). So $\{a,b\}$ lies in at least two Fibonacci sets.

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $b=2a$ and $F$ contains $a,2a$. By the Lemma (with $y=2a\le2x$, $x=a$) they are consecutive members: $a=x_i$, $2a=x_{i+1}$. If $i\ge2$, then $x_{i-1}=x_{i+1}-x_i=a=x_i$, contradicting $x_{i-1}<x_i$. So $i=1$ and $F=\{a,2a,\ldots\}$ is unique. ∎

arml-2003-power-03.title: Use the lemma
arml-2003-power-03.body:
Suppose a Fibonacci set $F$ contains $60,117,174$.

**Lemma (no members in between).** If $x<y$ are members of a Fibonacci set $F$ and $y\le2x$, then no member of $F$ lies strictly between them (so $x,y$ are consecutive members). *Proof.* Let $x=x_i$, $y=x_l$ and suppose $x_i<x_k<x_l$ for some $k$. Then $i<k<l$, and $y=x_l\ge x_{k+1}=x_k+x_{k-1}\ge x_k+x_i>2x$, contradicting $y\le2x$.

Since $174\le2\cdot117=234$, the members $117$ and $174$ are consecutive: $117=x_k$, $174=x_{k+1}$. Then $x_{k-1}=174-117=57$ (and $k\ge2$ because $60<117$ must precede $117$). The members before $117$ are at most $57$, but $60$ lies strictly between $57$ and $117$, so it cannot be a member. Contradiction. ∎

arml-2003-power-04.title: One Diophantine equation for each $n$
arml-2003-power-04.body:
Writing $f_1=f_2=1,f_3=2,\dots$ for the usual Fibonacci numbers, $x_n=f_{n-2}x_1+f_{n-1}x_2$ for $n\ge3$ (and $x_2$ for $n=2$). For each $n$ count the solutions of $f_{n-2}x_1+f_{n-1}x_2=2003$ with $1\le x_1<x_2$:

* $n=2$: $x_2=2003$; solutions $x_1=1,\dots,2002$ — 2002.
* $n=3$: $x_1+x_2=2003$; solutions $x_1=1,\dots,1001$ — 1001.
* $n=4$: $x_1+2x_2=2003$; solutions $x_1=1,3,\dots,667$ — 334.
* $n=5$: $2x_1+3x_2=2003$; solutions $(1+3t,\,667-2t)$ — 134.
* $n=6$: $3x_1+5x_2=2003$; solutions $(1+5t,\,400-3t)$ — 50.
* $n=7$: $5x_1+8x_2=2003$; solutions $(7+8t,\,246-5t)$ — 19.
* $n=8$: $8x_1+13x_2=2003$; solutions $(5+13t,\,151-8t)$ — 7.
* $n=9$: $13x_1+21x_2=2003$; solutions $(20,83),(41,70)$ — 2.
* $n=10$: $21x_1+34x_2=2003$; solutions $(29,41)$ — 1.
* $n=11$: $34x_1+55x_2=2003$; solutions $(12,29)$ — 1.

For $n=5,\dots,8$ the integer solutions form an arithmetic family $(x_1,x_2)=(x_1^0+f_{n-1}t,\ x_2^0-f_{n-2}t)$, and we keep those with $1\le x_1<x_2$ (for $n=7$: $7+8t<246-5t$ gives $t\le18$, so $t=0,\dots,18$). For $n\ge12$ the solutions have $x_1>x_2$ (for $n=12$ the smallest is $(17,12)$), so there are none.

Total: $2002+1001+334+134+50+19+7+2+1+1=3551$. (A direct computer enumeration confirms this.)

**Answer: 3551**

arml-2003-power-05.title: Every $i$ gives one
arml-2003-power-05.body: For every $i\ge1$: $x_{i+2}=x_i+x_{i+1}$ and $x_{i+3}=x_{i+2}+x_{i+1}=x_i+2x_{i+1}$. So $\{x_i,\ x_{i+2},\ x_{i+3}\}=\{a,a+d,a+2d\}$ with $a=x_i$ and $d=x_{i+1}$. Different $i$ give different subsets (the smallest element $x_i$ is increasing in $i$), so there are infinitely many. ∎

arml-2003-power-06.title: Use the lemma twice
arml-2003-power-06.body:
Suppose a Fibonacci set $F$ contains $a<a+d<a+2d<a+3d$.

**Lemma (no members in between).** If $x<y$ are members of a Fibonacci set $F$ and $y\le2x$, then no member of $F$ lies strictly between them (so $x,y$ are consecutive members). *Proof.* Let $x=x_i$, $y=x_l$ and suppose $x_i<x_k<x_l$ for some $k$. Then $i<k<l$, and $y=x_l\ge x_{k+1}=x_k+x_{k-1}\ge x_k+x_i>2x$, contradicting $y\le2x$.

Now $2(a+d)=2a+2d>a+2d$ and $2(a+2d)=2a+4d>a+3d$, so by the Lemma $a+d,a+2d$ are consecutive members and $a+2d,a+3d$ are consecutive members. Thus $a+d,a+2d,a+3d$ are three consecutive terms $x_k,x_{k+1},x_{k+2}$, so $a+3d=(a+d)+(a+2d)=2a+3d$, which gives $a=0$, contradicting $a>0$. ∎

arml-2003-power-07a.title: Work modulo 15
arml-2003-power-07a.body: The linear set $\{8,23,38,\dots\}$ has common difference $15$, so every member is $\equiv8\pmod{15}$. The Fibonacci set $7,11,18,29,47,76,123,199,322,\dots$ has residues mod $15$: $7,11,3,14,2,1,3,4,7,11,\dots$ — after the pair $(7,11)$ reappears the residues repeat with period $8$ (the recurrence determines each residue from the previous two). None of the residues $7,11,3,14,2,1,3,4$ equals $8$. So the sets have no common member. ∎

arml-2003-power-07b.title: Periodicity modulo $d$
arml-2003-power-07b.body:
Let the linear set have first term $k$ and difference $d$; it consists exactly of the integers $\ge k$ that are $\equiv k\pmod d$.

Consider a Fibonacci set $x_1,x_2,\dots$ reduced modulo $d$. There are only $d^2$ possible pairs $(x_i,x_{i+1})\bmod d$, so some pair repeats: $(x_i,x_{i+1})\equiv(x_j,x_{j+1})$ for some $i<j$. The recurrence can be run backwards ($x_{n-1}=x_{n+1}-x_n$), so $(x_{i-1},x_i)\equiv(x_{j-1},x_j)$, and so on down to $(x_1,x_2)\equiv(x_{j-i+1},x_{j-i+2})$. Therefore the whole sequence is periodic mod $d$ with some period $P=j-i$: $x_{n+P}\equiv x_n$ for all $n$.

Suppose a Fibonacci member $x_m$ is in the linear set, so $x_m\equiv k\pmod d$ and $x_m\ge k$. Then $x_{m+jP}\equiv k\pmod d$ for every $j\ge0$, and $x_{m+jP}\ge x_m\ge k$, so each of these infinitely many distinct members is in the linear set. Hence if the sets share one member they share infinitely many; "finitely many but at least one" is impossible. ∎

arml-2003-power-08a.title: Interleaving
arml-2003-power-08a.body: Take $F=\{3,4,\ldots\}=\{3,4,7,11,18,\dots\}$ and $G=\{3,5,\ldots\}=\{3,5,8,13,21,\dots\}$. They have the first member $3$ in common, and $x_2=4<y_2=5<x_3=7$. **Lemma I (interleaving).** Let $F=\{x_i\}$ and $G=\{y_i\}$ be Fibonacci sets with a common member $b=x_q=y_s$, and suppose $x_{q+1}<y_{s+1}<x_{q+2}$. Then $x_{q+k}<y_{s+k}<x_{q+k+1}$ for all $k\ge1$; in particular $F$ and $G$ have no common member larger than $b$. *Proof.* The case $k=1$ is the hypothesis. For $k=2$: $y_{s+2}=y_{s+1}+y_s>x_{q+1}+x_q=x_{q+2}$ and $y_{s+2}<x_{q+2}+x_{q+1}=x_{q+3}$ (as $y_s=x_q<x_{q+1}$). For $k\ge3$, assuming $x_{q+k-2}<y_{s+k-2}<x_{q+k-1}$ and $x_{q+k-1}<y_{s+k-1}<x_{q+k}$, we get $y_{s+k}=y_{s+k-1}+y_{s+k-2}>x_{q+k-1}+x_{q+k-2}=x_{q+k}$ and $y_{s+k}<x_{q+k}+x_{q+k-1}=x_{q+k+1}$. ∎ Applying Lemma I with $b=3=x_1=y_1$ (here $q=s=1$, and the hypothesis $x_2<y_2<x_3$ holds) shows $F$ and $G$ have no further common member. So their only common member is $3$. ∎

arml-2003-power-08b.title: Skip a term
arml-2003-power-08b.body:
Let $F=\{x_i\}=\{1,2,3,5,8,\dots\}$ and $G=\{y_i\}=\{1,3,4,7,11,\dots\}$, so $y_1=x_1$, $y_2=x_3$. In general take $y_1=x_i$, $y_2=x_j$ with $j\ge i+2$.

Then $y_3=x_i+x_j<x_{j-1}+x_j=x_{j+1}$ (as $x_i\le x_{j-2}<x_{j-1}$), and $y_4=y_3+y_2=x_i+2x_j>x_j+x_{j-1}=x_{j+1}$. So $y_3<x_{j+1}<y_4$ with common member $b=x_j=y_2$. **Lemma I (interleaving).** Let $F=\{x_i\}$ and $G=\{y_i\}$ be Fibonacci sets with a common member $b=x_q=y_s$, and suppose $x_{q+1}<y_{s+1}<x_{q+2}$. Then $x_{q+k}<y_{s+k}<x_{q+k+1}$ for all $k\ge1$; in particular $F$ and $G$ have no common member larger than $b$. *Proof.* The case $k=1$ is the hypothesis. For $k=2$: $y_{s+2}=y_{s+1}+y_s>x_{q+1}+x_q=x_{q+2}$ and $y_{s+2}<x_{q+2}+x_{q+1}=x_{q+3}$ (as $y_s=x_q<x_{q+1}$). For $k\ge3$, assuming $x_{q+k-2}<y_{s+k-2}<x_{q+k-1}$ and $x_{q+k-1}<y_{s+k-1}<x_{q+k}$, we get $y_{s+k}=y_{s+k-1}+y_{s+k-2}>x_{q+k-1}+x_{q+k-2}=x_{q+k}$ and $y_{s+k}<x_{q+k}+x_{q+k-1}=x_{q+k+1}$. ∎ Apply Lemma I with the roles of the two sets exchanged ($G$ first, $F$ second; $b=y_2=x_j$): it shows no later member is common. The members of $G$ before $y_2$ consist only of $y_1=x_i$, which is in $F$. So the common members are exactly $y_1$ and $y_2$. For the example: $F\cap G=\{1,3\}$. ∎

arml-2003-power-09a.title: The two smallest common members are consecutive in both
arml-2003-power-09a.body:
Let $F=\{x_i\}$, $G=\{y_i\}$ be Fibonacci sets with more than two common members, and let $a<b$ be their two smallest common members. **Lemma I (interleaving).** Let $F=\{x_i\}$ and $G=\{y_i\}$ be Fibonacci sets with a common member $b=x_q=y_s$, and suppose $x_{q+1}<y_{s+1}<x_{q+2}$. Then $x_{q+k}<y_{s+k}<x_{q+k+1}$ for all $k\ge1$; in particular $F$ and $G$ have no common member larger than $b$. *Proof.* The case $k=1$ is the hypothesis. For $k=2$: $y_{s+2}=y_{s+1}+y_s>x_{q+1}+x_q=x_{q+2}$ and $y_{s+2}<x_{q+2}+x_{q+1}=x_{q+3}$ (as $y_s=x_q<x_{q+1}$). For $k\ge3$, assuming $x_{q+k-2}<y_{s+k-2}<x_{q+k-1}$ and $x_{q+k-1}<y_{s+k-1}<x_{q+k}$, we get $y_{s+k}=y_{s+k-1}+y_{s+k-2}>x_{q+k-1}+x_{q+k-2}=x_{q+k}$ and $y_{s+k}<x_{q+k}+x_{q+k-1}=x_{q+k+1}$. ∎

*Claim: $a,b$ are consecutive members of both $F$ and $G$.* Write $b=x_q=y_s$ and let $c=x_{q-1}$, $c'=y_{s-1}$ be the preceding members; $c,c'<b$ and $c,c'\ge a$, with $c=a$ exactly when $a,b$ are consecutive in $F$ (similarly for $c'$ and $G$).

* If $c>a$ and $c'>a$: then $c\ne c'$ (otherwise $c$ would be a common member strictly between $a$ and $b$). Say $c<c'$. Then $x_{q+1}=b+c<b+c'=y_{s+1}<2b+c=x_{q+2}$ (using $c'<b$), so Lemma I applies and there is no common member above $b$.
* If $c>a$ and $c'=a$: $y_{s+1}=b+a<b+c=x_{q+1}<2b+a=y_{s+2}$ (using $c<b$), so Lemma I (with the roles exchanged) applies.
* If $c=a$ and $c'>a$: symmetric to the previous case.

In each of these cases there would be no common member above $b$, so only $a,b$ would be common, contradicting "more than two". Hence $c=c'=a$.

So $a=x_p=y_r$ and $b=x_{p+1}=y_{r+1}$, and by the recurrence $x_{p+t}=y_{r+t}$ for all $t\ge0$. Every common member is $\ge a$ (minimality), and the members of $F$ that are $\ge a$ are exactly $x_p,x_{p+1},\dots$, which all lie in $G$. So the common members are $a,b,a+b,a+2b,\dots$, which is the Fibonacci set $\{a,b,\ldots\}$. ∎

arml-2003-power-09b.title: Counting argument
arml-2003-power-09b.body: In a Fibonacci set $x_1\ge1$, $x_2\ge2$ and $x_{k}=x_{k-1}+x_{k-2}\ge2x_{k-2}$, so $x_{2j+1}\ge2^j$ and $x_{2j+2}\ge2^{j+1}$; thus $x_k\ge2^{(k-1)/2}$. If $x_k\le N$ then $k\le2\log_2N+1$. So each Fibonacci set has at most $2\log_2N+1$ members not exceeding $N$, and $F_1,\dots,F_n$ together have at most $n(2\log_2N+1)$ members up to $N$. Since $N/\log_2N\to\infty$, for $N$ large enough $n(2\log_2N+1)<N$, so some integer in $\{1,\dots,N\}$ belongs to none of the sets. ∎

arml-2003-power-10.title: Zeckendorf shift
arml-2003-power-10.body:
Let $F_2=1,F_3=2,F_4=3,F_5=5,\dots$ be the Fibonacci numbers. By Zeckendorf's theorem every positive integer $N$ has a unique representation $N=\sum F_{k_i}$ with $k_i\ge2$ pairwise non-consecutive. Define the *shift* $S(N)=\sum F_{k_i+1}$ (this is again a Zeckendorf representation).

* $S$ is injective (uniqueness of representations) and $S(N)>N$.
* $S(S(N))=\sum F_{k_i+2}=\sum(F_{k_i+1}+F_{k_i})=S(N)+N$.
* A number $M$ is in the image of $S$ iff its representation has no $F_2=1$ (smallest index $\ge3$): then $M=S(M')$ where $M'$ lowers every index by $1$. Call the numbers whose representation contains $F_2$ *roots*; they are exactly the numbers not in the image of $S$. There are infinitely many roots ($1$, $4=3+1$, $6=5+1$, $9=8+1$, $12$, $\dots$).

For a root $r$ let $F_r=\{r,S(r),S^2(r),\dots\}$. Then $r<S(r)$ and by the second bullet applied to $S^{n}(r)$, $S^{n+2}(r)=S^{n+1}(r)+S^n(r)$, so $F_r$ is a Fibonacci set. Every positive integer $M$ lies in some $F_r$: lower all its indices until the smallest is $2$, getting a root $r$ with $M=S^t(r)$. The sets are pairwise disjoint: if $S^a(r)=S^b(r')$ with $a\ge b$ then injectivity gives $S^{a-b}(r)=r'$, impossible for a root $r'$ unless $a=b$ and $r=r'$.

So the positive integers are partitioned into infinitely many Fibonacci sets: $\{1,2,3,5,\dots\}$, $\{4,7,11,18,\dots\}$, $\{6,10,16,26,\dots\}$, $\{9,15,24,\dots\}$, $\{12,20,32,\dots\}$, and so on. The answer is **yes**. ∎
